title: What do A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, and C2 mean?
invitation: Those small level codes appear on books, classes, tests, and language profiles around the world. Here is what they are actually trying to tell you, and how Gef uses them.
summary: Gef uses CEFR A1 through C2 as a common map for language ability, keeps Pre-A1 for first steps, and adds a clearly labeled Fully fluent / Native self-description above C2 in Gef's own picker. Your real ability can still be different in reading, listening, speaking, writing, interaction, and mediation.

blocks.title: A common map for language ability
blocks.text: A1 through C2 come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, usually called CEFR. It gives learners, teachers, schools, tests, and publishers a shared way to talk about language ability. A and B are not school grades. The scale moves from early basic communication through increasingly independent, flexible, and precise language use. Gef uses those coordinates because the same basic map can work across many languages without pretending that every language has the same vocabulary or grammar path.

blocks.title: Pre-A1 · First steps
blocks.text: Pre-A1 is the space before A1. You may recognize a few words, signs, sounds, names, numbers, or memorized expressions while still needing substantial support. Modern CEFR materials include Pre-A1, so Gef does not need to invent A0 as an official-sounding level. Gef keeps Pre-A1 for lessons, diagnostics, and early progress. In the simple self-rating slider, though, the center means no knowledge and the first outward ring is A1, keeping the visual scale easy to understand.

blocks.title: A1 · Beginner
blocks.text: At A1, you can do useful things with a small amount of language. Familiar topics and concrete situations are your strongest territory. You may understand short simple material, exchange basic information, recognize common language in context, and get an immediate need across. Support still matters, and unfamiliar situations can become difficult quickly. Moving toward A2 means making your language less dependent on memorized scripts and becoming comfortable with a wider set of ordinary situations.

blocks.title: A2 · Everyday
blocks.text: At A2, routine life starts becoming manageable in the language. You can usually get the main meaning from short straightforward material and communicate basic information about familiar people, places, activities, work or school, shopping, travel, time, and immediate needs. You are still working with limited range, but you can do more than repeat prepared lines. Moving toward B1 means connecting ideas across longer stretches, handling less predictable situations, explaining simple reasons, and relying less on somebody else to carry the exchange.

blocks.title: B1 · Independent
blocks.text: B1 is where independent use becomes much more visible. You can manage many ordinary situations without planning every sentence in advance. On familiar subjects, you can follow the central meaning of clear extended language and produce connected communication about experiences, plans, preferences, opinions, and problems. You will still meet gaps and misunderstandings, but they do not end every conversation or text. Moving toward B2 means increasing range, detail, speed, and control so more complex material stays workable.

blocks.title: B2 · Strong independent
blocks.text: At B2, you can take part effectively in sustained communication and deal with substantially more complex language. You can follow and discuss ideas that are concrete or abstract, explain a position in detail, and operate in many social, academic, and professional situations without requiring constant simplification. Errors and gaps still exist, but you have enough range to work around many of them. Moving toward C1 means gaining finer control of inference, nuance, register, organization, and style.

blocks.title: C1 · Advanced
blocks.text: At C1, the language becomes a flexible tool rather than a constant obstacle. You can handle demanding material, follow meaning that is not always stated directly, and communicate at length with strong organization and precision. You can adapt to many social, academic, and professional settings and make deliberate choices about tone and style. Moving toward C2 is less about collecting one final set of grammar rules and more about depth: subtle distinctions, rapid reformulation, specialized domains, cultural range, and precise control when language becomes unusually complex.

blocks.title: C2 · Highly proficient
blocks.text: C2 is the highest common CEFR reference level. A C2 user can handle exceptionally demanding language with very fine control of meaning, structure, implication, and style across a broad range of situations. C2 does not mean knowing every word, never making an error, or changing your identity into a native speaker. Languages are too large for that. Even experts and lifelong speakers meet unfamiliar vocabulary and unfamiliar fields.

blocks.title: Fully fluent / Native · Gef's top self-description
blocks.text: Gef adds one more stop above C2 in its own self-rating control: Fully fluent / Native. This is not CEFR C3 and it is not an official external certification. It is a practical choice for someone whose current command in that skill is mature, broad, automatic, and comparable to a fully fluent adult native speaker. Being born into a language does not automatically place a child at the top of every skill, and a non-native speaker can choose this level if the description genuinely fits. Gef is describing ability here, not ancestry.

blocks.title: Your language ability is a shape, not one letter
blocks.text: A single level is convenient, but real ability is uneven. Gef can keep six separate axes: Reading, Listening, Speaking, Writing, Interaction, and Mediation. You might read at C1, understand speech at B2, write at B1, and speak at A2. A heritage speaker may understand family conversations easily while finding formal writing difficult. None of that is contradictory. A six-sided radar graph makes those differences visible instead of sanding them down into one fake-perfect number.

blocks.title: What is mediation?
blocks.text: Mediation is helping meaning cross a gap. Translation and live interpreting are obvious examples, but it is broader than that. You are mediating when you summarize a difficult text for someone who cannot use the original, explain an idea in simpler language, relay information between people who do not share a language, reframe a disagreement so both sides understand it, or combine information from several sources into something another person can use. It measures how well you can help meaning travel, not merely how many words you can translate.

blocks.title: Gef currently measures reading, not your whole hexagon
blocks.text: Gef is a reading-first app today. You can tell Gef your own estimate for all six skills, but books, reading lessons, comprehension, and dictionary behavior may contribute evidence only to your Reading estimate. Gef must not quietly decide how well you speak, listen, write, interact, or mediate from things you did while reading. Those other axes are ready for future features without pretending those features already exist.

blocks.title: An A2 book tells you about the book
blocks.text: If Gef marks a book A2, that is a reading-difficulty signal. It means the language in the book is intended to be around A2 reading demand. Finishing that book is useful evidence about your reading, but it does not suddenly prove that your speaking, listening, writing, interaction, and mediation are also A2. The same rule applies to tests: always ask what ability was actually measured. A level without its scope can sound more certain than the evidence really is.

blocks.title: The world has several language-level systems
blocks.text: CEFR is not the only scale. ACTFL is widely used in United States language education. The Interagency Language Roundtable, or ILR, uses a 0-to-5 scale in U.S. government contexts. Canada uses the Canadian Language Benchmarks for English and NCLC for French. Japanese learners often meet the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, or JLPT, with levels N5 through N1. Mandarin Chinese learners may meet HSK, the Chinese Proficiency Test, which is currently transitioning toward a newer nine-level system. These systems were built for different purposes, so Gef keeps them distinct instead of pretending every label has one perfect twin.

blocks.title: A useful example: the Japanese JLPT
blocks.text: Beginning with the December 2025 Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, a passing score report can include a CEFR reference level based on the JLPT test level and total score. The important catch is scope: JLPT tests language knowledge, reading, and listening. It does not test speaking, writing, or interaction. So even an official cross-reference should update only what the evidence actually covers. This is exactly why Gef stores skill profiles instead of turning every certificate into one giant global level.

blocks.title: Chinese HSK is changing, so dates matter
blocks.text: HSK is standardized Mandarin Chinese proficiency testing. A newer HSK 3.0 model is designed around three stages and nine levels, but rollout has been transitional: the January 2026 Levels 1–6 event was announced as a pilot, while the official notice said regular 2026 exam dates would continue under HSK 2.0 until the formal launch is announced. This is why Gef stores framework versions and dates instead of baking a viral conversion chart into permanent app code.

blocks.title: A framework is not the same thing as a test
blocks.text: CEFR is a framework for describing proficiency. Different exams, schools, and organizations can design assessments and relate their results to it. A test score therefore needs context: which skills were tested, how the test was linked to the framework, when that relationship was established, and whether the result is official or only approximate. Gef can estimate progress for learning purposes, but it should never present an app estimate as an official CEFR certification.

blocks.title: There is no universal A2 word count
blocks.text: Vocabulary matters, but CEFR does not define A1, A2, or B1 by one universal number of words. Language-specific researchers create separate reference inventories because languages organize meaning differently. Even the meaning of one 'word' changes with segmentation, scripts, compounds, and morphology. An English vocabulary estimate cannot simply be copied onto Japanese, Arabic, Turkish, Mandarin, or every other language. Gef researches vocabulary and grammar targets separately by language and treats them as evidence and learning guidance, not as the definition of the level.

blocks.title: How Gef uses the levels
blocks.text: Gef uses CEFR A1 through C2 as the common coordinate system, with Pre-A1 for first steps and one Gef-only Fully fluent / Native self-description at the top of the manual picker. Books carry reading difficulty. Learner profiles can keep six skill values. A level badge can open this lesson directly at the relevant section. Language-specific curriculum data can then describe useful concepts, vocabulary senses, grammar patterns, scripts, and text types at that stage without blindly translating an English word list.

blocks.title: A Gefstimate is an estimate, not a diploma
blocks.text: When Gef eventually combines repeated evidence into its own estimate, English can call that a Gefstimate. The joke will not be forced into every language: some languages have a wonderfully compatible word for estimate and others do not. Under the joke, the meaning stays serious. A Gefstimate is Gef's best evidence-based estimate of current ability in a particular skill. It is not an official CEFR certificate, and Gef should always be able to explain what evidence contributed to it.

blocks.title: How do you move to the next level?
blocks.text: Not by filling one magic progress bar. Future Gef estimates should look for repeated evidence across different material and situations. Vocabulary growth and grammar knowledge can support that evidence, but neither becomes a single gate. One easy book should not promote you. One difficult day should not demote you. The useful signal is a pattern over time: broader understanding, less assistance, greater range, and more control. Automated placement and adaptive testing are future infrastructure, not something today's reader should pretend it already measures.

blocks.title: The short version
blocks.description: Zero means no knowledge yet. Pre-A1 describes first steps. A1 and A2 build basic everyday ability. B1 and B2 mark growing independence. C1 and C2 describe advanced, flexible, precise proficiency. Gef then offers Fully fluent / Native as its own top self-description. Your real ability is the six-sided shape of what you can actually do.
